paragraphs: Masked self-supervised learning trains a model to predict hidden parts of data from the parts it can see. Because training combines many different masking patterns, the learned relationships form a matrix describing how coordinates help predict one another. This paper studies that combined predictor, making it the central object of its mathematical analysis.

The analysis considers a high-dimensional setting in which sample count grows proportionally with data dimension. Within this regime, the authors derive explicit generalization-error expressions and characterize the predictor’s spectral structure. For spiked covariance models, they identify a phase transition: recovery of latent signals begins across a mathematically characterized boundary.

The paper also identifies structured settings where masked learning provably outperforms principal component analysis. This establishes an advantage under those settings, rather than a universal ranking of the methods. Together, the results explain how masking objectives can extract underlying structure and specify circumstances in which their benefits extend beyond classical unsupervised learning.
icml-2026-a-random-matrix-theory-of-mask.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis identifies when masked self-supervised learning recovers latent signals and structured settings where it provably outperforms PCA.

paragraphs: Remote sensing images must preserve physical measurements as well as visual appearance. The paper addresses diffusion models whose generated imagery can look realistic while containing distorted spectral information or inconsistent radiometric values. AnyBand-Diff incorporates spectral priors and physical constraints into a framework for image generation and recovery of missing spectral bands.

Its masked conditional diffusion model uses two stochastic masking mechanisms to learn reconstruction from arbitrary subsets of bands. During sampling, a differentiable physical model supplies gradients that guide denoising toward physically plausible solutions. A separate physical loss applies constraints at pixel, region, and whole-image scales, connecting local reconstruction quality with broader consistency.

The reported experiments support the framework’s effectiveness in generating reliable imagery and accurately reconstructing spectral information. The approach matters because scientific usefulness depends on preserving relationships grounded in physics, beyond producing convincing pictures. Its contribution combines flexible conditioning on available bands with physical guidance during sampling and constraints operating across multiple spatial scales.
icml-2026-anyband-diff-a-unified-remote-.tldr: AnyBand-Diff combines masked diffusion with physical guidance to generate remote sensing imagery and reconstruct missing spectral bands.

paragraphs: Language-model agents often learn to reason with a fixed collection of external tools. That setup makes adaptation harder when tools change or unfamiliar ones become available. AutoTool trains agents to choose tools dynamically throughout a reasoning process, treating tool selection as a repeated decision that must remain consistent across multiple steps.

Training has two phases. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning first stabilize reasoning trajectories. A regularized ranking objective then refines tool choices. The authors also construct 200,000 examples containing explicit explanations for tool selections, covering more than 1,000 tools and over 100 tasks in mathematics, science, programming, and multimodal reasoning.

Across ten benchmarks, AutoTool-trained Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B models outperform the compared agents and integration methods despite using fewer parameters. Reported average gains range from 4.5% for search-based question answering to 7.7% for code generation. The models also use previously unseen tools during inference, supporting the claim that training can improve adaptability to evolving tool collections.
icml-2026-autotool-dynamic-tool-selectio.tldr: AutoTool trains language-model agents to select tools throughout reasoning and reports stronger performance and generalization to unseen tools.

paragraphs: Numerically precise answers expose a mismatch in standard language-model training. Cross-entropy treats numeric tokens as separate categories, without representing how close their numerical values are. This paper introduces Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or SMMD, to make the training objective sensitive to numerical distance and relationships among nearby numeric predictions.

SMMD defines distance-based similarities over the numeric portion of the vocabulary. It uses these similarities to match the predicted distribution with the target distribution. It also constructs a graph from those relationships and smooths the difference between prediction and target across that graph. These two components encourage distributional alignment and local numerical consistency.

The authors evaluate the objective on mathematical reasoning, arithmetic, clock-time recognition, and chart question answering using multiple open-weight language and vision-language models. SMMD consistently improves accuracy over cross-entropy and the compared numeric-target losses. Their analyses indicate that distribution matching and smoothness contribute complementary benefits, while the design of the numerical-distance kernel is important to the improvements.
icml-2026-enhancing-numerical-prediction.tldr: SMMD improves numerical prediction by training with numerical-distance relationships and a smoothness constraint over numeric tokens.

paragraphs: Long contexts require large key-value caches, which store information used by a language model’s attention mechanism. Compressing context into a text summary can discard information needed later. Earlier work showed that directly training a compact cache can preserve full-context performance, but its end-to-end optimization is slow and expensive.

This paper proposes Attention Matching, which constructs compact keys and values by matching what attention produces. At the level of individual key-value heads, it aims to reproduce attention outputs while preserving attention mass. This formulation breaks the compaction problem into simpler subproblems, some with efficient closed-form solutions, reducing the need for costly optimization.

The authors develop several methods within this framework and report an improved tradeoff between compaction time and retained quality. On some datasets, they achieve up to 50-fold compaction in seconds with little quality loss. Those qualifiers matter: the finding demonstrates substantial compression in evaluated settings, while the central methodological contribution is a faster way to preserve attention behavior.
icml-2026-fast-kv-compaction-via-attenti.tldr: Attention Matching builds compact KV caches quickly, achieving up to 50-fold compaction in seconds with little quality loss on some datasets.

paragraphs: Proving polynomial inequalities becomes difficult as the number of variables and polynomial degree increase. Symbolic methods offer strong guarantees, but searching for a suitable proof certificate can become expensive. NSPI combines language-model suggestions with symbolic computation to address this search problem while retaining a path to exact, machine-checked mathematical proofs.

The language model first proposes an approximate decomposition of a polynomial into a sum of squares. Symbolic computation then refines that proposal into an exact representation, which proves the target inequality. The resulting proof is certified in Lean. Each stage serves a distinct purpose: heuristic discovery proposes structure, exact algebra establishes the certificate, and formal checking verifies the proof.

Experiments on challenging benchmarks containing polynomials with up to ten variables support the method’s effectiveness and scalability. The result concerns this certificate-based pipeline and the evaluated problems. Its significance is that approximate model-generated mathematical ideas can become useful starting points for a process whose final output is an exact, formally certified proof.
icml-2026-from-llm-generated-conjectures.tldr: NSPI turns language-model proposals for polynomial sum-of-squares decompositions into exact certificates and Lean-checked inequality proofs.

paragraphs: Spatial representations are useful for navigation only if they can guide movement. This paper develops a mathematical framework connecting patterns resembling the brain’s spatial codes with a policy for reaching goals. It starts from principles of representational smoothness and efficiency, seeking a shared explanation for both representing an environment and acting within it.

The authors show how diverse spatial codes arise from spectral decompositions of the Laplace operator. They then derive a navigation policy using a Green’s function potential. This potential reflects the environment’s intrinsic geometry, allowing an agent to follow its gradient in a way that takes the shape of the environment into account.

The framework improves sample efficiency and generalization in goal-reaching tasks, and its spectral representations can be learned from high-dimensional visual inputs. These findings support both practical navigation and learning from sensory experience. The authors interpret them as suggesting a spectral account of the cognitive map that is consistent with observed spatial-code patterns, rather than establishing the brain’s actual mechanism.
icml-2026-from-representation-to-action-.tldr: A Laplacian framework links spatial representations to geometry-aware navigation and reports improved learning efficiency and generalization in goal-reaching tasks.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning starts with existing data and then adapts through fresh interaction. Constraints that encourage caution during offline learning can become poorly matched to changing behavior during fine-tuning. This paper argues that deciding how to handle a sample solely from whether it came from offline or online collection can therefore be misleading.

DARE adjusts constraints according to each sample’s behavioral consistency with a behavior model. A posterior-based exchange mechanism reorganizes samples into offline-like and online-like subsets using that consistency. Because the framework needs only a per-sample alignment measure, it can be built on many offline algorithms with different behavior models and fine-tuning objectives.

The theoretical analysis shows that behavior-based exchange consistently improves the distinction between those subsets. On D4RL experiments, DARE improves fine-tuning stability and final performance over strong offline-to-online baselines. The contribution is a distribution-aware basis for relaxing constraints as behavior evolves, connecting the training objective more closely to what individual samples represent during adaptation.
icml-2026-from-static-constraints-to-dyn.tldr: DARE relaxes reinforcement-learning constraints using each sample’s behavioral alignment, improving offline-to-online fine-tuning in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graph learning becomes harder when nodes lack attributes, because graph neural networks typically depend on that information. Existing generative approaches can struggle with unstable training and fail to represent the range of attribute patterns compatible with graph structure. GLAD uses latent diffusion to generate missing attributes conditioned on the graph’s connections.

The framework aligns structure and attributes in both directions. During training, a structure reconstruction constraint encourages generated representations to retain information about connections. During sampling, structure-aware classifier-free guidance steers attribute generation toward consistency with the graph. Together, these mechanisms connect plausible attribute values with the topology they are supposed to describe.

The authors show theoretically that GLAD optimizes a tighter variational lower bound on joint log-likelihood than GAN-based predecessors, with better mode coverage. Large-scale benchmark experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in attribute recovery and downstream tasks. These findings indicate that preserving structure–attribute relationships can improve both the reconstructed data and the usefulness of that data for graph learning.
icml-2026-glad-bidirectional-structure-a.tldr: GLAD completes missing graph attributes with latent diffusion and bidirectional structural alignment, improving recovery and downstream performance in experiments.

paragraphs: Recovering a full physical system from partial observations can leave several possible explanations for the same measurement. Even when the complete state evolves according to Markovian dynamics, partial observations can make the reconstruction depend on history. This paper addresses that ambiguity by using observation sequences to initialize an evolving reconstruction.

The proposed HB-ARFM method uses conditional flow matching to build the initial reconstruction from observation history. It then reuses the same conditional transport model autoregressively, combining new observations with earlier predictions to advance through time. History therefore helps resolve the starting ambiguity, while past predictions supply continuing context as subsequent states are reconstructed.

The authors evaluate the method on boiling dynamics, recovering full velocity and temperature fields from interface geometry and motion. Across two inverse tasks with different observation sparsity, it produces physically and temporally valid reconstructions where the compared models fail. The findings support using temporal information throughout reconstruction when individual observations do not identify the hidden physical state.
icml-2026-history-bootstrapped-flow-matc.tldr: HB-ARFM uses observation history and past predictions to reconstruct boiling velocity and temperature fields from partial interface observations.

paragraphs: Vector quantization compresses visual or audio representations using a collection of discrete codes. Large, unstructured codebooks can be used inefficiently, with some codes receiving little use and codebook collapse reducing the effective representation. IVQ addresses this problem by building organization into the codebook itself, drawing inspiration from IChing.

The design combines binary hierarchical composition with geometric symmetry relationships. This gives a compact collection of codes a structured way to represent the latent space. The intended benefit is to maintain broad code use without collapse while reducing the size of the codebook needed for useful representations.

In audio experiments, IVQ achieves better quality with substantially smaller codebooks and consistently higher utilization than several vector-quantization variants. Additional experiments on visual reconstruction and cross-modal generation support its applicability beyond audio. These results make the codebook’s internal organization central to the contribution: a smaller structured vocabulary can represent signals effectively when its available codes are used more fully.
icml-2026-ivq-structured-and-lightweight.tldr: IVQ organizes discrete codes through binary hierarchy and symmetry, reporting better audio quality with smaller, more fully used codebooks.

paragraphs: Irregular event sequences provide scattered observations of systems that continue changing between events. An individual’s hidden state may evolve alongside broader population changes, with the two processes influencing each other at different times. CoCLD models this interaction jointly, addressing approaches that separate these processes or approximate them using discrete time steps.

The framework aligns individual latent dynamics and population-level distributional shifts in a continuous-time latent space. It combines a diffusion-based latent interpolator with neural ordinary differential equations. This supports interpolation, generation, and alignment of hidden states at arbitrary times, giving the coupled processes a common representation despite asynchronous and sparse observations.

The authors show that their coupling mechanism yields a consistent estimator of continuous-time latent dynamics under sparse, irregular observations. Empirical evaluations cover next-event prediction, mobility trajectory generation, and sequential behavior modeling. The reported results indicate that explicitly connecting individual and population dynamics helps capture dependencies across these tasks, supporting the usefulness of joint continuous-time modeling for irregular event data.
icml-2026-learning-coupled-continuous-ti.tldr: CoCLD jointly models individual and population dynamics in continuous time to learn from sparse, irregular event sequences.

paragraphs: Adapting a vision-language model through prompt learning becomes unreliable when training labels are wrong. Filtering or rebuilding those labels can propagate mistakes. Evidence-Prompt starts from the authors’ observation that pretrained embeddings remain resilient to label noise, making them useful references even though their direct adaptation to a new task is limited.

The method frames prompt learning as Bayesian reasoning. It combines evidence that does not depend on the supplied supervision with evidence conditioned on that supervision, using both to assess credibility and infer training targets. This lets stable pretrained knowledge contribute to adaptation while the model learns from potentially unreliable labels.

Across eight benchmarks with synthetic and real-world label noise, Evidence-Prompt consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods and makes accuracy degrade less sharply as noise rises. At 75% noise on OxfordPets, reported gains are 36.6% under asymmetric noise and 14.4% under symmetric noise. Incorporating the evidence prior into other methods also improves accuracy, supporting its usefulness beyond the proposed framework.
icml-2026-leveraging-evidence-priors-for.tldr: Evidence-Prompt combines stable pretrained knowledge with supervision-dependent evidence to improve prompt learning when labels are noisy.

paragraphs: LiveOIBench evaluates language models on difficult competitive programming tasks with extensive official tests and direct comparisons to elite human contestants. It addresses gaps in existing coding benchmarks, including insufficiently challenging problems, limited test coverage, and dependence on online platform interfaces. Evaluation runs fully offline, supporting reproducible assessment without those platform dependencies.

The benchmark contains 403 expert-curated problems from 72 contests across 14 Informatics Olympiads held between 2023 and 2025. Problems average 60 official test cases and include detailed subtask scoring rubrics. Continuous updates are intended to reduce contamination risk, while the human comparisons put model scores in the context of actual contest performance.

Among 34 evaluated models, GPT-5 reaches the 81.76th percentile, below the top human contestants; open-weight GPT-OSS-120B reaches the 60th percentile. Reasoning-trace analysis associates robust reasoning with precise problem analysis over excessive exploration. Analyses of release timing, task familiarity, and code similarity find minimal evidence of contamination, supporting the benchmark’s evaluation value without establishing that contamination is absent.
icml-2026-liveoibench-can-large-language.tldr: LiveOIBench provides offline Olympiad-level coding evaluation and finds that tested models still trail the strongest human contestants.

paragraphs: Some useful training objectives provide no reliable gradient for backpropagation, including hard classification error and black-box feedback. Likelihood-ratio methods offer an alternative, but their estimates can have high variance in large spaces. OVLR addresses that instability by moving perturbation and sampling into the lower-dimensional space of model outputs.

The framework uses antithetic sampling, pairing perturbations to reduce estimator variance. It requires a single deterministic forward pass, with additional sampling costs confined to repeated loss evaluations. This design makes direct optimization of gradient-agnostic objectives more practical without repeatedly evaluating the full network for each sampled loss.

Experiments span classification, generative modeling, language modeling, robot imitation learning, and black-box optimization. OVLR remains competitive where backpropagation supplies useful gradients and enables objectives such as hard 0-1 loss for noise-tolerant classification and truncated losses for outlier-resistant regression. The results support output-space variance reduction as a way to expand the objectives that modern deep networks can practically optimize.
icml-2026-ovlr-efficient-scalable-and-ro.tldr: OVLR reduces likelihood-ratio estimator variance through output-space sampling, enabling training with objectives that lack useful gradients.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that better prediction and optimization alone are insufficient foundations for heart transplant allocation policy. Allocation decisions involve organizations and people whose incentives can differ, including procurement organizations, transplant centers, clinicians, patients, and regulators. A policy therefore operates within an interacting decision system where strategic behavior matters.

Focusing on adult heart transplant allocation in the United States, the authors identify incentive misalignments across the decision pipeline. They also present data indicating that these misalignments already have adverse consequences. This motivates treating incentives as part of the problem that an allocation policy must address when using machine learning and data-driven optimization.

The proposed research agenda brings together mechanism design, strategic classification, causal inference, and social choice. The authors call for these perspectives to support robust, efficient, fair, and trusted allocation in the presence of strategic behavior. The contribution is a case for incentive-aware policy development and a research direction, rather than a reported demonstration of a completed replacement allocation system.
icml-2026-position-machine-learning-for-.tldr: The authors argue that heart transplant allocation policies must account for participants’ incentives and strategic behavior.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that sustainable AI requires attention to economic and social conditions alongside environmental impact. Its central tension concerns access: broader access to development infrastructure can support AI sovereignty and equity, while expanding use of that infrastructure also carries environmental costs. Considering either side in isolation leaves this conflict unresolved.

The authors examine these tensions through the base-superstructure framework from historical materialism, focusing on how material conditions shape AI development and the discussion around it. They argue that failing to reconcile climate awareness with resource awareness contributes to a global AI arms race. This is the paper’s analytical position about the consequences of the current development pattern.

The proposed Climate and Resource Aware Machine Learning framework, CARAML, organizes recommendations across individual, community, industry, government, and global levels. Its purpose is to bring environmental concerns and equitable access into a shared sustainability agenda. The contribution is a framework for confronting the tradeoff across levels of action, with economic and social sustainability included explicitly.
icml-2026-position-neglecting-the-sustai.tldr: The paper argues that sustainable AI must reconcile equitable infrastructure access with environmental costs and proposes CARAML to guide action.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that uncertainty about a prediction cannot be fully understood without uncertainty about the input’s domain. It considers three sources: epistemic uncertainty, aleatoric uncertainty, and domain uncertainty. The authors contend that analyses focused on the first two overlook whether an input itself is valid for the modeled setting.

Their proposed representation combines the distribution of inputs given training data with the conditional distribution of outputs given inputs and training data. Multiplying these produces the joint distribution of inputs and outputs. In the authors’ account, the input distribution represents domain uncertainty, while the conditional distribution supplies the predictive part of the representation.

The paper also echoes findings that information-theoretic uncertainty methods can be suboptimal both within and outside the training distribution, particularly because epistemic and aleatoric components are difficult to separate. Its central claim is that the joint distribution provides the coherent representation needed to include all three sources. This is presented as a position on uncertainty representation for responsible decision-making.
icml-2026-position-predictive-uncertaint.tldr: The authors argue that joint input–output modeling is needed to represent domain, epistemic, and aleatoric uncertainty coherently.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that AI alignment methods have a dual-use problem: mechanisms developed to prevent harmful responses may also help malicious actors censor information or manipulate users. Its central concern is that improving control over a model’s outputs can serve both protective purposes and deliberate efforts to control what people learn.

The authors connect existing alignment techniques with possible misuse and actual cases of misuse. They use this mapping to argue that the pursuit of increasingly aligned models also gives malicious actors increasingly capable tools for informational control. The argument concerns intentional misuse of alignment mechanisms; it does not establish that every use of alignment produces censorship.

The paper presents this concern as urgent because more people are turning to AI for information. It argues that unequal economic power and political movement toward authoritarianism further increase the risk. The authors call on the alignment community to account for deliberate misuse and propose mitigation strategies. Their broader message is that evaluating alignment requires attention to how its mechanisms could be repurposed, alongside their intended role in preventing harm.
icml-2026-position-the-alignment-communi.tldr: This position paper argues that AI alignment methods can also enable censorship and manipulation, and calls for safeguards against deliberate misuse.

paragraphs: This position paper questions whether immediate user approval is a suitable objective when people ask language models about relationships, difficult decisions, or long-term goals. In these settings, what someone wants to hear may differ from what benefits them over time. The authors propose a widely accessible, optional mode explicitly optimized and evaluated for long-term well-being.

Their motivation draws on findings described in the abstract: models endorse questionable framings above human baselines, people readily accept AI advice without improved well-being, and sycophantic models can increase dependence while reducing prosocial intent. These concerns support evaluating assistance beyond whether a particular reply pleases the user in the moment.

The proposal has three principles: change the objective, let users choose explicit relational roles, and avoid paternalism. It organizes design around when well-being is measured, whose interests count, and how the assistant participates. This makes choices currently embedded implicitly in model behavior explicit, while preserving user choice through an opt-in design and attention to the assistant’s role.
icml-2026-position-we-need-large-languag.tldr: The authors propose an opt-in language-model mode optimized for long-term well-being, with explicit user-selected roles and safeguards against paternalism.

paragraphs: Predicting several future tokens has been proposed as an extra training objective for language models, but its benefits have been inconsistent. The authors find that identifying exact future tokens is too difficult as an auxiliary task. They instead introduce token order prediction, which trains a model to rank upcoming tokens by how soon they appear.

This ranking objective provides a different way to learn from future context alongside next-token prediction. It requires one additional unembedding layer, compared with the multiple transformer layers used by multi-token prediction. The paper compares training objectives across models with 340 million, 1.8 billion, and 7 billion parameters.

Across nine standard language benchmarks, token order prediction performs better overall than next-token prediction, multi-token prediction, and DeepSeek multi-token prediction. Benefits also appear on four math and code benchmarks after continued training. On a synthetic star-graph task, it enables pathfinding where the compared objectives fail. These results support relative token order as an effective auxiliary signal across the evaluated scales and tasks.
icml-2026-predicting-the-order-of-upcomi.tldr: Training models to rank upcoming tokens by proximity improves language modeling overall across the evaluated model sizes and benchmarks.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent limits each training example’s gradient and adds Gaussian noise. Its usefulness depends strongly on the clipping threshold, which can require repeated calibration when fixed. SlaClip adapts that threshold using slack information produced by the standard clipping operation, treating an existing training signal as an indicator for adjustment.

The method uses a post-hoc Slack Indicator without making an additional private query. Under the same training configuration and privacy accountant, it preserves vanilla DP-SGD’s sampling rule, noise multiplier, and global sensitivity bound. It is accounted for using the same per-step privacy bound, making those shared conditions central to its privacy claim.

Experiments across diverse datasets and tasks show consistent improvements over the compared adaptive clipping baselines. The significance is a practical adaptation mechanism that fits into DP-SGD and its variants without separate private monitoring of gradient statistics. By extracting useful information from clipping itself, the method addresses threshold sensitivity while retaining the stated privacy accounting and core training configuration.
icml-2026-slaclip-gradient-norm-slacks-c.tldr: SlaClip adapts DP-SGD clipping thresholds using existing slack information without additional private queries under the stated accounting conditions.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning can be expensive when every available example is used, and it can sometimes amplify bias or overfit. Online batch selection chooses examples dynamically during training. This paper develops Utility-Diversity Sampling, or UDS, to consider both how useful an example is and how much diversity it contributes to the selected data.

UDS uses the nuclear norm of the logits matrix to capture utility and diversity within a sample. It estimates diversity between samples through comparisons of low-dimensional embeddings, keeping a lightweight memory of historical examples. This design avoids dependence on external reference models or validation sets and eliminates unnecessary backpropagation associated with selection.

Across multiple benchmarks and data budgets, UDS consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art online batch selection methods. It also substantially reduces training time relative to fine-tuning on the full dataset. The results support making diversity part of the selection rule while keeping that rule inexpensive enough for selecting fewer examples to yield an actual training-time benefit.
icml-2026-utility-diversity-aware-online.tldr: UDS selects fine-tuning examples using utility and diversity, improving on compared selection methods while reducing full-dataset training time.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds generation by having a draft model propose token sequences for a target model to verify. This paper identifies a mismatch: draft training often optimizes a single greedy trajectory, while decoding verifies and ranks multiple sampled paths. Variational Speculative Decoding trains around the probability that proposed sequences will be accepted.

VSD treats draft paths as latent proposals and derives a variational lower-bound objective that rewards useful proposals while reducing divergence from the target distribution. It adds a path-level utility and uses expectation-maximization. The expectation step samples an oracle-filtered posterior using MCMC; the maximization step fits weighted likelihood with adaptive rejection weighting and confidence-aware regularization.

The theoretical analysis establishes increases in expected acceptance length and speedup. Experiments across language and multimodal language models report speedups of up to 9.58% over EAGLE-3 and 8.80% over ViSpec. These are maximum reported improvements. The central contribution is aligning draft training with sequence acceptance, the behavior that directly determines how much speculative decoding can accelerate generation.
icml-2026-variational-speculative-decodi.tldr: VSD trains speculative draft models for sequence acceptance and reports up to 9.58% speedup over EAGLE-3 and 8.80% over ViSpec.

paragraphs: Understanding a long video requires finding useful information among thousands of frames within a limited computation budget. Uniform sampling can miss important content, while a single keyframe-selection pass cannot recover from poor choices. VideoBrain trains a vision-language model to acquire additional visual information adaptively and judge whether it has seen enough.

The framework combines two complementary agents. A CLIP-based agent retrieves frames by semantic relevance across the video, while a Uniform agent samples densely within time intervals. The vision-language model directly inspects frames and reasons about information sufficiency. A behavior-aware reward and data classification pipeline teach it when invoking these agents is beneficial, discouraging indiscriminate calls.

Across four long-video benchmarks, VideoBrain improves over the baseline by 3.5% to 9.0% while using 30–40% fewer frames. It also shows strong cross-dataset generalization to short-video benchmarks. The findings suggest that learned decisions about where and when to look can improve understanding while reducing the visual information a model needs to process.
icml-2026-videobrain-learning-adaptive-f.tldr: VideoBrain learns when and where to sample video frames, improving reported benchmark performance while using 30–40% fewer frames.
